paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Stratified sampling is a way of sampling a population that can be split into smaller groups. Each group is called a stratum, and before any sampling the members are sorted into strata whose members are alike. When the groups differ from one another, it can pay to sample each one on its own.

paragraphs.heading: The ground rules
paragraphs.text: The strata must cover everyone with no overlap: each member of the population is placed in exactly one stratum. A sample is then drawn inside every stratum, for example by simple random sampling.

paragraphs.heading: Why bother
paragraphs.text: The aim is greater precision, by cutting down sampling error. The method can give a weighted mean that varies less than the plain average of a simple random sample of the whole population. It is generally used when the population is not one uniform group. It gives a smaller error when measurements inside each stratum are less spread out than across the population as a whole.

paragraphs.heading: Three towns
paragraphs.text: Suppose we want to estimate the votes for each candidate in a country with three towns: 1 million factory workers live in Town A, 2 million office workers in Town B, and 3 million retirees in Town C. One random sample of 60 from the whole country might by chance be badly balanced across the towns, which would bias the estimate. Drawing 10 people from A, 20 from B and 30 from C instead gives a smaller error with the same 60 people.

paragraphs.heading: How many from each group
paragraphs.text: One way to share out the sample is proportionate allocation, where each stratum's sampling fraction matches its share of the population. Another is optimum allocation, also called disproportionate allocation, which also takes into account how spread out the variable is in each stratum. It draws bigger samples where variability is highest, to keep the overall sampling variance as low as possible. Neyman allocation is one strategy of this kind.

paragraphs.heading: Uneven regions and a trap
paragraphs.text: Stratifying also helps when population density varies a lot across a region. A survey of Ontario might sample a larger fraction in the thinly settled north, because a fraction set for the province as a whole could collect only a handful of data there. Merging small strata to get enough numbers needs care. It can lead to Simpson's paradox, where trends seen in separate groups vanish or even reverse once the groups are put together.
